hints: Merging two sorted lists is easy. Merging them one at a time into a growing result is O(N·k). Can you do better?
At each step the next node is the smallest among the k current heads. Which structure gives the minimum quickly?
A min-heap of (value, list index, node): pop the smallest, push its successor. Or merge lists in pairs, like merge sort.

insight.mnemonic: Only the k fronts can be next.
insight.oneLiner: Keep the k current heads in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest and push its successor.

recall.a: (value, list index, node) - the index breaks ties so nodes are never compared.
Divide and conquer: merge lists in pairs, halving the count each round.

insight.why: The heap never holds more than k nodes, so each of the N nodes costs O(log k): O(N log k) overall.

oneLiner: Keep the k current heads in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest and push its successor.

pitfalls.explain: On equal values, Python compares the next tuple element. Put a tiebreaker (the list index) before the node.
pitfalls.title: Heap compared ListNode objects

pitfalls.explain: Some lists can be empty (None) and the array itself can be empty.
pitfalls.title: Crashed on empty lists

solutions.idea: Gather every node, sort by value, relink. Ignores that the lists are already sorted.
solutions.name: Collect and sort

footnotes.text: Pairwise rounds halve the number of lists each time, so each node is merged about log k times: O(N log k), like the heap but with no extra memory.

solutions.idea: Repeatedly merge pairs of lists, halving their number each round.
solutions.name: Merge in pairs

footnotes.text: The index i breaks ties between equal values. ListNode objects can't be compared with <, so a tie must never fall through to comparing nodes.

solutions.idea: A min-heap of the k current heads yields the next smallest node in O(log k).
solutions.name: Min-heap of heads
